newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: More rebels head for Bougainville/PNG talks in NZ.
newsitem.headline: More rebels head for Bougainville/PNG talks in NZ.

text.p: Three more secessionist rebels from Papua New Guinea's Bougainville Island have left the Solomon Islands en route to peace talks in New Zealand, officials said on Tuesday.

They said the trio, including the central commander of the Bougainville Revolutionary Army (BRA), Ismael Torama, were able to cross from Bougainville to the Solomons with the cooperation of their enemies of nine years of fighting, the PNG military.
"Their departure from South Bougainville is being facilitated by PNG forces, which is good," a source close to the talks told Reuters.

Representatives of the three main groups in the Bougainville war, the PNG-backed Bougainville Transitional Government (BTG), the Bougainville Interim Government (BIG) and its associate the BRA, began discussions on Monday at Burnham Military Camp, near the South Island city of Christchurch.
New Zealand is providing logistical support but is not an official participant in the talks, which were only envisaged as involving representatives of the island.
A spokeswoman for Foreign Minister Don McKinnon, who set up the conference, said he was expecting more delegates to arrive throughout the week to join the 50 already in place.

According to officials working at the forum, a total of eight BRA delegates, stranded after apparent "friendly fire" downed the helicopter meant to bring them out last weekend, were now on their way via the Solomons route, among them Torama.

Another four people are due from the rebel stronghold of Buka Island, off Bougainville, and officials also expect two PNG politicians representing the resource-rich territory to travel soon from Port Moresby.
They are Sam Akoitoi, the member of parliament for central Bougainville, and former provincial secretary John Siau.

Thousands have died in the bloody Bougainville conflict since landowners revolted in 1988 over environmental damage caused by the huge Panguna copper mine, and the royalties they received from it. The mine is owned by a unit of the Anglo-Australian giant RTZ Corp.
Optimism surrounds the talks, despite the absence of shadowy BIG leader Francis Ona and the poor track record of previous attempts.

BIG/BRA delegation leader Joseph Kabui has said the efforts since the early 1990s to solve the Bougainville war were marred by time and process constraints, and implied that the circumstances may be more favourable this time.
It is understood that delegates are discussing the creation of a neutral zone on the island, policed by a Pacific peacekeeping force and where substantive peace negotiations can take place.
However, Ona has refused to attend previous internationally brokered talks and has so far failed to honour commitments made by his representatives.
These talks, expected to last at least a week, are also taking place against a background of uncertainty in PNG politics in the aftermath of a recent general election.
It has seen Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan and a clutch of other ministers lose their seats in the aftermath of a mercenary scandal with its roots in the Bougainville conflict.
Chan triggered the nation's biggest political crisis since independence when his US$36 million plan to use African mercenaries to end the rebellion was revealed in March and sparked an army revolt.
